title: How to get the list of dates or global min/max timestamp from an openEO DataCube without downloading all data?
q_body: I'm working with openEO Python client and a multi-temporal satellite DataCube. I want to extract either: The list of all timestamps in the cube, or The global minimum and maximum dates across the temporal dimension. So far, I've tried: min_cube = cube.min_time() max_cube = cube.max_time() But these only collapse the temporal dimension and return a DataCube, not the actual dates. Moreover, when I visualize the results, it seems min and max might not correspond to chronological min/max: for example, in 2025 it shows more vegetation in the “min” result than in the “max”, when in Northern Hemisphere min should be in the winter and max for today (Oct2 2025) should be in September. I also checked: cube.metadata.extent["temporal"] But it returns something like ['2015-07-04T00:00:00Z', None] — just the declared collection bounds, not the actual dates present. title: Python enum.Flag : best practice for creating "empty" and "full" flags
q_body: What is the "best" (as in, most likely to be intended and least likely to be deprecated/removed) way to create empty and full flags from enum.Flag ? Given the code: from __future__ import annotations import enum class Color(enum.Flag, boundary=enum.STRICT): RED = enum.auto() GREEN = enum.auto() BLUE = enum.auto() @staticmethod def black() -> Color: return Color(0) @staticmethod def white() -> Color: return Color(-1) print(Color.black()) # Color(0) print(Color.white()) # Color.RED|GREEN|BLUE Are Color(0) and Color(-1) the best way to create an empty/full flag respectively? The documentation does explicitly use the Color(0) idiom, thrice, in fact. Twice[ 1 ][ 2 ] in notices about changing "The repr() of zero-valued flags", and once[ 3 ] in an example for the __bool__ operator. I'm relatively comfortable about using this in production code, although I'd appreciate a more explicit "blessing" from the documentation for this idiom. Nevertheless, the Color(-1) is something I believe I haven't seen anywhere. As evidenced by the code, it works correctly even when the enum class has a STRICT boundary defined in its initialization. Is this "safe" for production usage? How much at risk is this of being deprecated/removed? Here are a few alternatives I've come up with: functools.reduce(operator.and_, Color) , for black , analogously with operator.or_ for white .
